messages.content:
RoadDraft is a headless 2D CAD engine for roadway plans. Model space is US survey feet, and a point is [x, y] = [easting, northing] -- the other way round from how coordinates are usually spoken, so N 7300, E 4100 is [4100, 7300]. Sheets are paper inches seen through viewports at a feet-per-inch scale. Work through the commands: each one validates its params and explains what was wrong, every change is journaled and undoable. Start with get_document_state to see what is in the document, list_commands for the full surface, and render_sheet or render_model to look at your work.

To annotate something, find it before you point at it. In a sheet file the design usually lives in a referenced basefile, so the document owns no geometry of its own; find_entities searches the attachments too. Filter by what a thing IS -- layer, type, or its design anchor -- rather than dumping the document: find_entities {anchor: {kind: 'offset', offset: [-15, 15]}, visible_on: 'P-202'} is the pavement edges that sheet shows. Then pass the id straight to place_callout as target_entity, and the engine puts the leader tip on the geometry. Do not compute the point yourself: the midpoint of a curve's endpoints is not on the curve, and roadway linework runs parallel a few feet apart, so a hand-computed point usually lands on the wrong line rather than on nothing. If you do pass a raw target point, read the warning that comes back -- it names what the tip actually touched.

Some things are not entities at all -- a station, a PC, a point at an offset. Ask the design for those: list_alignments with include_references=true names a referenced alignment 'BASE:RTE-7', and station_to_xy, xy_to_station, resolve_anchor and get_design_data all accept that name and answer in host coordinates. To call one out, give place_callout a target_anchor ('86+50@15R', 'PC-2'; BC-2 and EC-2 name the PC and PT too) and that alignment name. Otherwise commands do not take it: nothing can be drawn, labelled or anchored to an alignment this document does not own.

Plan annotation belongs on the sheet, in paper inches, not in the model. Pass the sheet as place_callout's space and still name a model target -- target_entity or target_anchor: the engine sees it through the sheet's viewport (scale and twist included) and puts the tip where it shows on the paper. 'at' then runs along the part of the entity that sheet shows, since a pavement edge runs the whole project and a sheet shows one stretch. find_entities with visible_on gives each row a sheet_point, which is where that tip will land -- use it to choose a position for the text that is clear of the linework. Never work out a viewport by hand: model_to_sheet and sheet_to_model convert, and station_to_xy and point_on_entity take a sheet and answer in paper inches as well.

Drafting from a description works the same way: give the engine the description, not coordinates you worked out. A bearing and distance goes in as written -- create_alignment takes start + legs (each leg a bearing, azimuth or deflection and the distance to the next PI, with the radius of the curve at the PI it starts from), draw_traverse draws lines and curves course by course, and traverse computes the points without drawing. offset_entity copies linework parallel at a distance (one entity, or a chain offset as one path), fillet rounds the corner between two lines with a curve (a curb return), and measure with along gives distances along a line, chain or alignment and square off it. key_points and snap give the exact endpoints, intersections, centers and alignment design points (PI, BC, EC) to build on. Station-and-offset drafting is draw_station_offset with the stations and offsets given ('82+00@15R'). Linework drawn through something is cut back with trim (a point on the part to cut away) or run on with extend, not redrawn from computed points; break, join, lengthen, chamfer, copy, rotate, mirror, scale and array edit what is there. create_points sets COGO points, label_segments letters bearings and distances or L1/C1 tags with line and curve tables, place_along sets blocks or points at an interval, hatch fills an area (a point inside is enough), and area and get_entity read areas, lengths, bearings and curve data off the drawing.

Do one drafting task in a headless CAD engine called RoadDraft, using the tools you have been given. They are your ENTIRE tool surface.

Rules:
- Every change to the drawing must go through a tool call.
- The document is already open and saves itself after each command. Do not save it under another name.
- Nobody can answer questions. Work until you judge the task done, then stop and give your report.
- You have no calculator and no code execution. Any arithmetic you need, do yourself.

THE TASK:
Draw a building footprint on a new layer named BUILDING: a 60 ft by 40 ft rectangle. One corner is at N 1200.00, E 1500.00. From that corner the 60 ft side runs N 30°00'00" E, and the 40 ft side runs at a right angle to it, to the right (S 60°00'00" E).

When finished, reply briefly with:
1. What you created and drew (names, layers, key coordinates).
2. The tool calls that mattered, in order (tool name + the key arguments).
3. Anything that failed, confused you, or that you had to work around -- quote error messages. If you had to compute coordinates yourself, show the arithmetic.

messages.reasoning:
*   Goal: Draw a 60' x 40' building footprint.
    *   Layer: `BUILDING`.
    *   Starting Corner: N 1200.00, E 1500.00. In RoadDraft coordinate system [x, y] = [easting, northing], so this is `[1500.00, 1200.00]`.
    *   Side 1: 60 ft, bearing N 30°00'00" E.
    *   Side 2: 40 ft, bearing S 60°00'00" E (right angle to the first side, to the right).
    *   Closing the rectangle: The rectangle needs 4 sides.
        *   Side 1: From `[1500, 1200]` at N 30° E for 60 ft.
        *   Side 2: From end of Side 1, at S 60° E for 40 ft.
        *   Side 3: From end of Side 2, at a bearing perpendicular to Side 2 (which would be N 30° W or S 30° E? Let's trace: Side 1 is 30° N of E. Side 2 is 60° S of E. The angle between them is 30 + 60 = 90°. Correct. Side 3 must be the same bearing as Side 1 but opposite direction: S 30° W).
        *   Side 4: From end of Side 3 back to start.

    *   Step 1: Create layer `BUILDING`.
    *   Step 2: Set current layer to `BUILDING`.
    *   Step 3: Calculate the vertices or use `draw_traverse` / `draw_polyline`. `draw_traverse` is best for bearings and distances.

    *   Start point: `[1500, 1200]`.
    *   Leg 1: `N 30° E`, `60 ft`.
    *   Leg 2: `S 60° E`, `40 ft`.
    *   Leg 3: `S 30° W`, `60 ft`.
    *   Leg 4: `N 60° W`, `40 ft`. (Wait, let's check bearings: Side 1: 30. Side 2: 120. Side 3: 210. Side 4: 300. All are 90 deg increments. Correct).

    *   Wait, `draw_traverse` with `close=true` might be easier if I can provide the closed path.
    *   Or I can use `draw_polyline` if I calculate the points.
    *   Actually, `draw_traverse` is perfect.

    *   Start: `[1500, 1200]`
    *   Leg 1: `bearing="N 30°00'00\" E", distance=60`
    *   Leg 2: `bearing="S 60°00'00\" E", distance=40`
    *   Leg 3: `bearing="S 30°00'00\" W", distance=60`
    *   Leg 4: `bearing="N 60°00'00\" W", distance=40`
    *   Set `close=true`.

    *   Corner 1: `[1500, 1200]`
    *   Leg 1 (N 30 E, 60'):
        *   $\Delta x = 60 \cdot \sin(30^\circ) = 60 \cdot 0.5 = 30$
        *   $\Delta y = 60 \cdot \cos(30^\circ) = 60 \cdot 0.866025 = 51.9615$
        *   Corner 2: `[1530, 1251.9615]`
    *   Leg 2 (S 60 E, 40'):
        *   $\Delta x = 40 \cdot \sin(60^\circ) = 40 \cdot 0.866025 = 34.641$
        *   $\Delta y = 40 \cdot (-\cos(60^\circ)) = 40 \cdot (-0.5) = -20$
        *   Corner 3: `[1530 + 34.641, 1251.9615 - 20] = [1564.641, 1231.9615]`
    *   Leg 3 (S 30 W, 60'):
        *   $\Delta x = 60 \cdot (-\sin(30^\circ)) = -30$
        *   $\Delta y = 60 \cdot (-\cos(30^\circ)) = -51.9615$
        *   Corner 4: `[1564.641 - 30, 1231.9615 - 51.9615] = [1534.641, 1180]`
    *   Leg 4 (N 60 W, 40'):
        *   $\Delta x = 40 \cdot (-\sin(60^\circ)) = -34.641$
        *   $\Delta y = 40 \cdot (\cos(60^\circ)) = 20$
        *   Corner 1 (check): `[1534.641 - 34.641, 1180 + 20] = [1500, 1200]` (Perfect).

    *   `create_layer(name="BUILDING")`
    *   `set_current_layer(name="BUILDING")`
    *   `draw_traverse(space="model", start=[1500, 1200], legs=[{"bearing": "N 30°00'00\" E", "distance": 60}, {"bearing": "S 60°00'00\" E", "distance": 40}, {"bearing": "S 30°00'00\" W", "distance": 60}, {"bearing": "N 60°00'00\" W", "distance": 40}], close=true, polyline=true)`

    *Actually*, the prompt says: "The 60 ft side runs N 30°00'00" E, and the 40 ft side runs at a right angle to it, to the right (S 60°00'00" E)."
    If I use `draw_traverse` with `close=true`, I only need to provide the legs that close it.
    If I provide 4 legs and `close=true`, it might try to add a 5th leg or just validate. Let's check `draw_traverse` docs.
    `close=true` "reports how well a boundary closes... and, when drawing, add the closing course".
    So if I want to draw the rectangle, I should provide the legs and let it close, or provide the full path.
    If I provide:
    1. N 30 E, 60
    2. S 60 E, 40
    3. S 30 W, 60
    And `close=true`, it will calculate the return to start and add the 4th leg (N 60 W, 40).

    Wait, the prompt says: "One corner is at N 1200.00, E 1500.00. From that corner the 60 ft side runs N 30°00'00" E, and the 40 ft side runs at a right angle to it, to the right (S 60°00'00" E)."
    I will provide the first 3 legs and set `close=true`.

    Wait, checking the `draw_traverse` `legs` parameter: "each from where the last one ended".
    If I want a closed polygon, I should define the path.
    Let's just provide all 4 legs and `polyline=true` to ensure it's one object.

    Let's start.

The task is to draw a 60x40 rectangle.
Corner 1: [1500, 1200] (E, N)
Side 1: 60 ft, Bearing N 30°00'00" E.
Side 2: 40 ft, Bearing S 60°00'00" E (which is a right angle to side 1).

Let's calculate the vertices.
Vertex 1: [1500, 1200]
Vertex 2 (end of 60ft side):
$\Delta E = 60 \cdot \sin(30^\circ) = 60 \cdot 0.5 = 30$
$\Delta N = 60 \cdot \cos(30^\circ) = 60 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 60 \cdot 0.866025 = 51.9615$
Vertex 2: [1500 + 30, 1200 + 51.9615] = [1530, 1251.9615]

Vertex 3 (end of 40ft side from V2):
Bearing S 60°00'00" E.
$\Delta E = 40 \cdot \sin(60^\circ) = 40 \cdot 0.866025 = 34.641$
$\Delta N = 40 \cdot -\cos(60^\circ) = 40 \cdot -0.5 = -20$
Vertex 3: [1530 + 34.641, 1251.9615 - 20] = [1564.641, 1231.9615]

Vertex 4 (back to start):
From V3, we need to go back to V1.
Check bearing/distance from V3 to V1:
$\Delta E = 1500 - 1564.641 = -64.641$
$\Delta N = 1200 - 1231.9615 = -31.9615$
Wait, a rectangle should have parallel sides.
Side 1: N 30 E
Side 3 (opposite Side 1): S 30 W
Side 2: S 60 E
Side 4 (opposite Side 2): N 60 W

Let's re-calculate Vertex 4 from V3 using the correct bearing (N 60 W):
$\Delta E = 40 \cdot -\sin(60^\circ) = -34.641$
$\Delta N = 40 \cdot \cos(60^\circ) = 20$
Vertex 4: [1564.641 - 34.641, 1231.9615 + 20] = [1530, 1251.9615] ... No.
Let's use the relative offsets for the rectangle.
V1: [1500, 1200]
V2: V1 + [30, 51.9615] = [1530, 1251.9615]
V3: V2 + [34.641, -20] = [1564.641, 1231.9615]
V4: V3 + [-30, -51.9615] = [1534.641, 1180] ... something is wrong.

Ah, I see. The corners of the rectangle are:
V1: [1500, 1200]
V2: [1500 + 60*sin(30), 1200 + 60*cos(30)] = [1530, 1251.9615]
V3: [1530 + 40*sin(60), 1251.9615 - 40*cos(60)] = [1530 + 34.641, 1251.9615 - 20] = [1564.641, 1231.9615]
Wait, S 60 E is a right angle to N 30 E.
N 30 E has azimuth 30.
S 60 E has azimuth 120.
120 - 30 = 90. Correct.

Let's find V4 by going from V1 with the bearing S 60 E (or rather, from V3 with the bearing opposite to V2-V1).
The side V1-V2 is N 30 E. The opposite side V4-V3 should be S 30 W.
The side V2-V3 is S 60 E. The opposite side V1-V4 should be N 60 W.
Let's calculate V4 using V1 + (opposite of V2-V3).
V2-V3 is [34.641, -20].
So V4 should be V1 - [34.641, -20] = [1500 - 34.641, 1200 + 20] = [1465.359, 1220].
Wait, let's check the distance V4-V1.
$\Delta E = 1500 - 1465.359 = 34.641$
$\Delta N = 1200 - 1220 = -20$
This is the vector [34.641, -20], which is S 60 E.
So V4 is [1465.359, 1220].

Let's verify the sequence:
V1: [1500, 1200]
V2: [1530, 1251.9615] (60' at N 30 E)
V3: [1564.641, 1231.9615] (40' at S 60 E)
V4: [1534.641, 1180] ... no.
Let's redo V3 and V4.
V1: [1500, 1200]
V2: [1530, 1251.9615]
V3 (V2 + S 60 E 40'):
$\Delta E = 40 \cdot \sin(60) = 34.641$
$\Delta N = -40 \cdot \cos(60) = -20$
V3: [1530 + 34.641, 1251.9615 - 20] = [1564.641, 1231.9615]
V4 (V3 + S 30 W 60'):
$\Delta E = -60 \cdot \sin(30) = -30$
$\Delta N = -60 \cdot \cos(30) = -51.9615$
V4: [1564.641 - 30, 1231.9615 - 51.9615] = [1534.641, 1180]
Wait, if V4 is [1534.641, 1180], then V4 to V1 is:
$\Delta E = 1500 - 1534.641 = -34.641$
$\Delta N = 1200 - 1180 = 20$
Bearing: E -34.641, N 20. This is N 60 W.
Distance: $\sqrt{34.641^2 + 20^2} = \sqrt{1200 + 400} = 40$.
Correct!

So the vertices are:
1. [1500, 1200]
2. [1530, 1251.9615]
3. [1564.641, 1231.9615]
4. [1534.641, 1180]
(Close to [1500, 1200])

I will use `draw_polyline` to draw the rectangle on the 'BUILDING' layer.
